I11ISequential versus simultaneous calibration of many targetsINsrc/calibrate/calibrate.py:563 (simultaneous grid over the free set, CAL.search.max_rounds)noneThe field states the choice explicitly and it is a real fork, not a matter of taste. In dynamic OD calibration, 'the first formulation estimates the whole set of time-dependent OD matrices SIMULTANEOUSLY for the entire time period in one calibration round. The second formulation estimates and calibrates OD matrices SEQUENTIALLY one at a time for each time frame. Most optimization-based studies have used the simultaneous approach, since the available sequential methods may lose accuracy due to giving up some information in the transition between time frames' - while the simultaneous form 'is incapable of handling a stream of data for real-time or online demand calibration'. The same paper states the bind that makes the choice matter at all: 'this optimization problem is underdetermined for large-scale networks since the number of roads with traffic measurement is usually several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of all roads in the network', and it names the standard architecture as BI-LEVEL - an upper-level discrepancy minimisation over an inner assignment that must be re-solved at every candidate, where 'performing several DTAs for each optimization task demand considerable computational resources'. In DTA practice the sequential form is supply first and then demand with the supply held fixed; the reported weakness of decomposing is that the stages need not be internally consistent, because each stage's assumed input is not the other stage's output.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.173152026-09-09
I12IDamping and step-size schedule in the constant-adjustment contractionINsrc/calibrate/asc_fixed_point.py:112 (CAL.asc.max_step_utils 1.5, CAL.asc.damping 0.6)noneThe log-ratio ASC step is a contraction only if it is damped, and the two open implementations of it disagree on how. The leading open MATSim calibrator, matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools, computes the raw step verbatim as 'math.log(z_i) - math.log(m_i) - (math.log(z_0) - math.log(m_0))' and applies it under a SCHEDULE whose default is 'linear_scheduler(start=0.6, end=1, interval=3)' - the early rounds take 0.6 of the raw step and the fraction relaxes to the full step over three intervals, i.e. cautious while the shares are far from target and undamped once they are near. The agency practice in the ActivitySim world applies a FLAT dampener instead of a schedule. Neither publishes a convergence proof, and the same library's 'TerminationCondition.check_termination' still carries '# TODO: not used yet' - so the field's standard answer ships a damping default and no working stopping rule at all. The undamped step (1.0) is the boundary case: it is what a fixed point converges to when it converges, and what overshoots when the shares are far out.https://github.com/matsim-vsp/matsim-python-tools/blob/master/matsim/calibration/utils.py2026-09-09
I13IDiagnosing a residual: constant versus missing mechanismPARTIALsrc/analyse/measure_realisation_gap.py:2 (ride only); walk constant frozen as absorbing a routing failurewalkThe profession's own manual puts constant adjustment LAST and lists what must be exhausted first. FHWA's Travel Model Validation and Reasonableness Checking Manual, chapter 7 (Mode Choice / Vehicle Occupancy), states that 'simple adjustments to modal constants estimated using weighted samples should be considered "a last resort" after all other possible causes for error and calibration adjustments have been considered', and its Table 7.6 orders the checks ahead of it: verify trip distribution for the market segment, check that the implied transit share is reasonable, recheck the skim data (networks, time periods, geographic scope), consider revising the model STRUCTURE, evaluate indicator variables or adjust their coefficients - and only then revise an alternative-specific constant. The same chapter states plainly that 'there are no applicable criteria guidelines for checks of mode choice', so the field supplies an ORDER of diagnosis and no numeric bar. What it does not supply anywhere reached this pass is a TEST that separates the two cases: no source reviewed proposes reading the round-over-round behaviour of the constant update itself as the diagnostic.https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/planning/tmip/publications/other_reports/validation_and_reasonableness_2010/ch07.cfm2026-09-09
I14IMulti-objective aggregation across many simultaneous targetsINsrc/calibrate/calibrate.py:289 (CAL.objective.components goal_modes.max_abs_rel_pct)noneAggregating many targets into one number has a known and specific failure. Jakob and Blume set it out: with a weighted sum, 'by varying the weights, any point of a convex Pareto front can be obtained... On the other hand, it is possible that parts of the Pareto front cannot be found in case of a non-convex problem... the part between points A and B of the Pareto front cannot be obtained for any weights. This is a serious drawback.' The counterweight is cost: 'the computational effort to determine all or at least most of the Pareto front increases significantly with the number of conflicting objectives', and the paper's framing is that the real-world question arises 'where either more than four objectives have to be considered, or the same type of task is repeated again and again with only minor modifications'. So beyond about four conflicting targets a full Pareto treatment is expensive and scalarisation is the practical route - while the scalarisation chosen decides which compromises are reachable at all. A weighted sum of squared deviations across targets is the standard form in simulation-based transport calibration.https://arxiv.org/pdf/2203.026972026-09-09
F5FRouter-scorer consistency: does the search optimise the utility the plan is scored by?PARTIALsrc/java/citysim/RaptorModeCostConfigGroup.java:125 (C.raptor.mode_cost_representation = absent): the raptor prices time and waits only, walk at 1.04x IVT, no fare, no constant, no incomelight rail -70 %, walk 4.54 kmMATSim's own choice-model chapter makes the split explicit: an agent's realised behaviour is P(i|U) = sum over choice sets of P(i|C) x P(C|U) - the choice model AND the way the choice set was generated. The router is the choice-set generator, so a router that optimises a different objective from the scoring function generates alternatives the scorer will then reject, and 'alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen'. MATSim's stock car routing keeps the two aligned by deriving the link travel cost from the scoring parameters (the negative marginal utility of travelling plus the marginal utility of performing); the alignment is deliberate and is broken wherever a specialised router is used. The SwissRailRaptor's DefaultRaptorInVehicleCostCalculator prices a boarded leg as in-vehicle seconds times one coefficient, so a per-submode constant, a fare or a crowding surcharge that lives only in scoring is invisible to the transit search that picks the submode.https://d-nb.info/1172809151/342026-09-10
H9HEquilibrium selection and the innovation cutoff: what the reported share is a share OFPARTIALsrc/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1303 (RUN.replanning.score_msa_representation = absent)car/walk snap at the cutoffMATSim's iterative loop is not stationary while innovation runs: its own terminology page states that 'as long as innovation is still switched on in MATSim (new routes, new times, ...), the result is not truly stationary', and that once innovation is disabled 'the result is indeed a stationary process, but limited to the set of plans that every agent has at that point in time'. The selection protocol before the cutoff 'resembles a MNL choice model', P(i|C) = exp(mu S_i)/sum exp(mu S_j) with mu = brainExpBeta, and the chapter notes that BestPlanSelector is the same selector with an infinite mu. So the pre-cutoff share is a logit-dispersed mixture over each agent's remembered plans and the post-cutoff share is the same population collapsed toward its arg-max: switching innovation off changes the estimator, not only the amount of search. Assignment theory says the same thing from the other side - a low dispersion parameter concentrates flow on the perceived-best alternative and the pattern approaches deterministic user equilibrium, which is the classic 'unrealistic route concentration' that stochastic user equilibrium was introduced to cure. The efficiency loss of that concentration is bounded and modest on real networks - a data-driven estimate for Eastern Massachusetts puts the price of anarchy near 1.30, and other empirical work finds it close to 1 in both light and heavy traffic - so an equilibrium being reached is no guarantee that it resembles the observed day, which is itself a non-equilibrium average.https://matsim.org/docs/userguide/terminology.html2026-09-10
H10HChoice-set coverage as a binding constraint on any constant or priceINsrc/analyse/report_choice_set_coverage.py:6; ride coverage 19.09 % against the 20.6 % target at it.229ride -13.7 %Flotterod and Kickhofer state the mechanism in one line and it is an identity, not a tendency: 'the generation of the choice sets affects the simulated choices. The simplest illustration of this mechanism is that alternatives that never appear in the choice set cannot be chosen. Similarly, including certain alternatives with a low (high) probability in the choice set decreases (increases) their probability of being chosen, given that the choice model is not changed.' They add the consequence for a calibration exercise directly: 'When a choice study's synthetic choice sets are very different from the alternatives considered in the real world, it is unlikely that the simulation will display correct aggregated quantities or useful sensitivities for policy measures', and that MATSim's mutation and innovation procedures 'constitute concrete, yet heuristic, approaches to the choice set generation problem' whose biases 'can, however, be difficult to quantify'. The plan memory is the other half of the constraint: the choice set is bounded by maxAgentPlanMemorySize, plans past it are deleted by a PlanSelectorForRemoval, and the MATSim user guide records that 'a problem is that the process that generates the choice set at this point is not systematic'. A mode constant therefore has an upper bound on what it can move that is set by the fraction of agents who ever held that mode in memory, not by its own magnitude.https://d-nb.info/1172809151/342026-09-10
H11HMode availability by distance: an upper bound on a walk or bike alternativeINERTsrc/java/citysim/GatedSubtourModeChoice.java:237 beyondReach; B.mode.walk_feasible_km and B.mode.bike_feasible_km SHIPPED AT THEIR OFF VALUE 0.0 (check_hardcoding.py section 7; results/raw/20260923T034632_250it_25pct/config.xml module modeAvailability)walk 4.54 km, bike 8.32 kmCycling distance is short and its distribution is well measured. Australian travel survey data for 2012-2020 put the median home-based cycling trip at 3.5 km, varying strongly by purpose - 1.8 km utilitarian, 5.3 km commuting, 3.7 km recreational - with trip purpose the strongest predictor and men cycling further than women. The Montreal metropolitan survey puts the 85th percentile of cycling distance at 5,517 m, and the 85th-percentile access distance is the field's usual way of setting a catchment. Distance decay for cycling fits an exponential or lognormal curve rather than a cliff, so the correct representation is a decaying utility rather than a hard cut-off - but a simulator that offers the mode at any distance with no decay term places mass far out in a tail the survey does not contain.https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11675929/2026-09-10
I15IDistributional targets beyond mode share: trip length, intrazonal share, occupancyPARTIALsrc/calibrate/fit.py:51 reads params/C4_mode_constraints.json into _fit.json trip_geometry_constraint - reported, never fitted (walk ratio 6.5, bike 1.60, pt 0.55)walk, bike, pt geometryThe profession does not accept a mode share as a model's validation on its own; it validates the distribution the share is drawn from. The standing guidance is explicit and numeric: 'Generally, the modeled average trip lengths for each trip purpose should be within five percent of observed for each trip purpose'; the trip length frequency distribution is compared as a whole using the coincidence ratio - 'the area under both curves divided by the area under at least one of the curves' - and 'it is preferable for the coincidence ratio for each trip purpose to be at least 70 percent'; and 'regionwide intrazonal trip percentages should be within three percentage points of observed for each trip purpose'. Vehicle occupancy has moved into the same class: in trip-based models the vehicle occupancy factor was an input converting person trips to vehicle trips, while 'in activity-based models (ABM), the role of VOF transitioned from a major input to a validation target for shared-rides'. On the assignment side the same manuals give volume tolerances by facility class - Ohio's VMT guidance is plus or minus 7 per cent on freeways and expressways, 10 per cent on principal and minor arterials, 15 per cent on collectors, with Michigan DOT at 5 and 10 per cent for screenlines and cutlines and Florida at 20 per cent for transit screenlines - while stating that 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards'.https://tfresource.org/topics/Model_Validation_and_Reasonableness_Checking_Distribution.html2026-09-10
K4KFlow-capacity, storage-capacity and stuck-time correction at a sample fractionPARTIALresults/raw/20260923T034632_250it_25pct/config.xml:47 stuckTime 10.0 (RUN.qsim.stuck_time_s, assumed); storage exponent 1.0carThe correction rules for a downscaled run are contested and were measured again this year. Mersini and Ziemke (MUM 2025, TU Berlin) set out the position: former recommendations scaled storage less than flow, flowCapacityFactor = sample share and storageCapacityFactor = sample share^alpha with alpha = 0.75 'to prevent breakdowns in small samples', while 'more recently, flow and storage capacities are usually scaled equally, i.e., with alpha = 1', the Open Berlin practice; Llorca and Moeckel found 'no substantial differences in average travel times for a given MATSim scenario when comparing different sample shares using both alpha values', and Ben-Dor, Ben-Elia and Benenson again recommend 0.75. Their measured result on a 100 per cent Lausitz benchmark is that scores and travel times are close to the full-scale run at 25 and 50 per cent, deviate at 5 per cent and clearly at 1 per cent, and that 'even average statistics (such as score and travel time) become unreliable when sampling below 10%'. The sharper finding is on the third parameter nobody scales: stuck-time violations, normalised by the inverse sample share, rise from about 40,000 at 100 per cent (about one agent in eight stuck once per day) to three times as many at 1 per cent, and with equal scaling of flow and storage 'even more than four and a half times as many' - so alpha = 1 costs stuck agents at small samples, and the paper flags that stuck time itself should be scaled with the sample size, larger for smaller samples.https://matsim.org/conferences/mum2025/abstracts/MUM25_paper_30.pdf2026-09-10
K5KExpanding a sampled run's link volumes for a counts comparisonPARTIALsrc/calibrate/fit.py:208 scale_error; counts expanded by the fractioncar countsA downscaled run's link volumes must be multiplied back before they mean anything against an observed count, and MATSim carries the factor as a first-class setting: countsScaleFactor 'represents a multiplier for scaling model results back to real-world volumes, so that when a model is based on a countsScaleFactor of 10, the real fleet sizes would be ten times higher'. The expansion is only the first of three basis decisions, and the other two are where practice models put their error bars: WHICH simulated vehicles count (the observed detector counts every vehicle class, so the modelled side must either add its heavy vehicles or the observed side must be converted to a light-vehicle basis - one or the other, never neither), and WHICH link a station maps to (a two-way station is the sum of both directions and a station matched to a service road or the wrong carriageway reads near zero). The tolerance guidance is by volume class rather than per link, and the manuals warn against reading it as a standard: 'the guidelines in this section should not be construed as standards; matching or exceeding the guidelines is not sufficient to determine the validity of a model.'https://tfresource.org/topics/Model_Validation_and_Reasonableness_Checking_Assignment.html2026-09-10
E25ERail bonus: the submode preference for rail over bus at equal servicePARTIALsrc/java/citysim/CitysimControler.java:629 raptor mode cost installs only when C.raptor.mode_cost_representation = mode_constant; ships absent; RUN.mode_choice.pt_submode_alternatives = aggregate, so C.asc.rail/-light_rail/-bus are scored but never steer the submodelight rail -70 % / heavy rail +57 %Across the comparative literature a rail vehicle attracts more riders than a bus offering the same travel time, frequency and walk distance: transport models find 5-15 % higher expected ridership for rail than for bus with similar characteristics, and Scherer and Dziekan measured a 'psychological rail factor' - a stated preference for rail at equal service - of 63 % for regional train and 75 % for tram against bus. Currie and Delbosc's BRT/LRT comparison attributes part of the gap to load factor, reliability, comfort and visibility, and part to perception. The consequence for a simulator is that a router which allocates a pt trip between bus and tram on time alone cannot reproduce an observed bus/tram split, whatever constants the plan-level scorer carries.https://www.worldtransitresearch.info/research/4219/2026-09-11
J6JAutomatic passenger counts, vehicle location and occupancy feeds as calibration dataPARTIALcities/newcastle/extract/extract_boam.py exists; no consumer in src/calibrate or src/analyse (grep)bus -13 %Where an agency instruments its buses, per-service occupancy and on-time running become observations a simulator can be scored against below the monthly contract total. TfNSW publishes BOAM (Bus Opal Assignment Model), 'an indicator of historic bus occupancy for individual bus services from January 2020' under Creative Commons Attribution, with a v2.0 field document behind login; its regional coverage is not stated on the page. Every Hunter and Lower North Coast bus has been fitted with GPS and automatic passenger counting under the Transport Connected Bus programme (233 buses), and PTIPS-based on-time running is published for Sydney Metropolitan and Outer Metropolitan contracts from 2010. GTFS-Realtime for the Hunter is live and can be archived by the user.https://opendata.transport.nsw.gov.au/dataset/boam-bus-opal-assignment-model2026-09-11
J7JBespoke aggregate tables from the travel survey where unit records are not releasedOUTno bespoke HTS table in the package; the request is drafted (#50) and unsentwalk/bike shape, taxi unfoldingTfNSW publishes the Household Travel Survey by Region, LGA and SA3 (2020/21-2024/25 released 9 March 2026; dashboards) and states that to protect respondents it is 'unable to provide the data in any alternative form or at a more granular level'; the same programme supplies BESPOKE tables - the dataset page says 'If you have been supplied bespoke journey data for historical years recently, please request updated tables' (contact opendataprogram@transport.nsw.gov.au). A model that cannot estimate on unit records can still request the specific cross-tabulation its target needs (mode by age band, trip-length distribution by mode, occupancy by purpose) for its study area.https://opendata.transport.nsw.gov.au/dataset/household-travel-survey2026-09-11
E26ECar: per-kilometre operating cost, congestion time, chain-based availabilityINsrc/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1524 (C.scoring.monetary_distance_rate car/ride -0.00018 AUD/m, derived); congestion time on the queue networkcar inside bandCar use is price-inelastic in the short run and elastic only over the long run and only with respect to TOTAL cost. The European review by de Jong and Gunn (2001), as tabulated by Litman, gives car-kilometres with respect to fuel price -0.16 short term and -0.26 long term (commuting -0.12 / -0.23), and car-kilometres with respect to travel time -0.20 short term and -0.74 long term; Goodwin (1996) gives urban-road vehicle travel with respect to travel time -0.27 short run and -0.57 long run. Litman's synthesis states the scaling explicitly: a -0.1 short-run elasticity of vehicle travel with respect to fuel price reflects a -0.3 long-run elasticity, which reflects about -1.2 with respect to total vehicle costs, because most vehicle costs (depreciation, financing, insurance, registration, residential parking) are fixed and short-run effects are about a third of long-run ones. Brons, Nijkamp, Pels and Rietveld's meta-analysis of gasoline-demand price elasticities (158 estimates) finds the demand response driven mainly by fuel efficiency and car ownership and to a lesser degree by mileage per car, with a long-run estimate about -0.46 for total fuel demand. On what a driver actually prices, the classic Transportation paper 'Perceived and actual costs of operating cars' finds the modal split consistent with drivers perceiving petrol costs only, which is why mode-choice models price car by a marginal per-kilometre cost rather than by full cost of ownership.https://www.vtpi.org/elasticities.pdf2026-09-14
H12HHabit, inertia and satisficing: does the agent re-optimise every day, or stick until a threshold is crossed?PARTIALresults/raw/20260923T034632_250it_25pct/config.xml:185 maxAgentPlanMemorySize 8 (RUN.replanning.max_agent_plan_memory) with ChangeExpBeta; no explicit inertianoneHabit is one of the two strongest predictors of the mode a person uses, and it is a MEASURED effect, not a residual. Three meta-analyses put the pooled correlation between a habit measure and the travel mode used at r+ = 0.50 (Gardner & Abraham 2008), r+ = 0.42 (Lanzini & Khan 2017, 58 primary studies) and r = 0.47 (Hoffmann et al. 2017), against an averaged pooled car-use-intention correlation of r+ = 0.83 in Lanzini & Khan; the review of reviews that collects them (Javaid, Creutzig & Bren d'Amour 2020) notes the differences between the meta-analyses exceed their confidence intervals. In discrete-choice terms inertia is the tendency to stick with the past choice even when another alternative becomes more appealing: Cherchi & Manca (2011, Transportation 38:679-695) test eight specifications on an RP/SP dataset with a mixed logit and find a significant, mode-specific inertia that weakens with learning across the SP experiments; Cantillo, Ortuzar & Williams (2007, Transportation Science) model it as a randomly distributed inertia THRESHOLD with serial correlation. The route-choice literature measures the same thing as an INDIFFERENCE BAND: travellers do not switch unless the saving exceeds a threshold (Mahmassani & Liu 1999), and Zhu & Levinson (2016, Transportation) estimate lognormal bands on 78 GPS subjects around the Minneapolis I-35W bridge replacement, which explains why the new bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving predicted. Satisficing (Simon 1957) is the general form - search stops at a satisfactory alternative - and boundedly rational user equilibrium (Di & Liu 2016 review) is the assignment that follows from it. The magnitudes the field reports are correlations and thresholds, not a utility constant; a simulator represents habit either as a state-dependent term (past mode in the utility), as a switching threshold, or - as MATSim does - as a selection rule over remembered plans.https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/aba0322026-09-14
F6FTravel-time reliability and route switching: the reliability ratio and the indifference band in route choiceOUTdeterministic travel times; reliability exists only in the unused ServiceQualityConfigGroup (src/java/citysim/ServiceQualityConfigGroup.java:32)noneReliability enters route choice as a second attribute beside mean time, and the field's summary statistic is the RELIABILITY RATIO - the value of a unit of standard deviation over the value of a unit of mean travel time. Carrion & Levinson (2012, TR-A 46(4):720-741) review and meta-analyse the estimates and attribute their spread to measurement (which dispersion measure, SP versus RP, self-reported versus GPS times). The same authors' Minneapolis before-and-after study of the I-35W bridge (39 subjects with complete data, 78 GPS observations) shows how far the ratio moves with measurement alone: 1.30 (mean/SD) and 1.60 (median/SD) on SELF-REPORTED times against 0.42 and 0.77 on GPS-MEASURED times, and 0.83 / 0.39 on the mean-to-90th-percentile measure - a ratio above 1 with perceived times and below 1 with measured ones. Route SWITCHING is boundedly rational: travellers keep their usual route until the saving exceeds an indifference band (Mahmassani & Liu 1999; Zhu & Levinson 2016 estimate lognormal bands on the same 78-subject GPS panel and use them to explain why the replaced bridge attracted less traffic than its time saving implied). For a simulator this means (a) a reliability term in route cost needs a measured day-to-day time variance per link, which a single-day equilibrium simulation does not produce, and (b) the switching rate of the route-choice strategy is itself a behavioural parameter.https://findingspress.org/article/8330-uncovering-the-influence-of-commuters-perception-on-the-reliability-ratio2026-09-14
B7BImmobility: the share of persons who make no trip on the survey dayPARTIALsrc/build/build_activity_chains.py:186 (B.activity.p_mandatory, assumed); no travelling-share constraint in fit.pytrip totals behind every shareMadre, Axhausen & Brog (Transportation 34, 2007) treat the immobile share - persons not leaving home on the reporting day - as both a central result and a prime quality indicator of a travel diary survey: for a standard one-day, weekday-only diary it should lie in the range 8-12 %, and a higher figure signals soft refusal (respondents claiming not to have left the house) rather than a behavioural fact. Later panel work (Transportation 2022, weekly routines of employees and retirees) shows immobile days cluster by person and weekday, so a one-day rate understates the share of people who are ever immobile and overstates the share of habitually immobile people.https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11116-006-9105-52026-09-16
E27EHeavy rail: station access mode - walk, feeder bus, park-and-ride, kiss-and-rideOUTswissRailRaptor intermodalAccessEgress carries walk only (results/raw/20260923T034632_250it_25pct/config.xml module swissRailRaptor); no park-and-ride or kiss-and-ride (grep: none)heavy rail +57 %, pt trip length 12.96 vs 23.4 kmStation access is a mode choice of its own and its split moves with distance and supply. In Sydney, walking is the access mode for about half of home-to-train trips and almost 90 % of home-to-bus trips (Daniels & Mulley 2013, from the HTS); TfNSW's rail-user analysis puts walk access at 48 % and walk EGRESS at 84 %, because the car is not available at the far end. Meng, Taylor & Scrafton (ATRF 2017) observed three Adelaide Gawler-line interchanges in 2010: Mawson Lakes - feeder bus 46 %, park-and-ride 27 %, kiss-and-ride 17 %, walk+bike 10 %; Elizabeth - bus 44 %, walk 37 %, park-and-ride 11 %, kiss-and-ride 7 %; Gawler (one occasional bus) - walk 43 %, park-and-ride 36 %, kiss-and-ride 15 %, bus 3 %. Their stated-preference model finds walking distance, bus access, bus waiting time, car access and car-park availability all significant, with age, income and gender effects. Outer-suburban Sydney stations surveyed by Ku-ring-gai Council read car-driver access at 35 % (17-52 % by station). The rule is that park-and-ride grows with distance from the CBD and with free station parking, and that a walk-only access model under-states the catchment of an outer station by roughly the car-access share.https://australasiantransportresearchforum.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/ATRF2017_114.pdf2026-09-16
E28EWalk-access distance to public transport: the catchment distribution behind a search radiusINsrc/build/build_matsim_run_inputs.py:1970 (RUN.transit_router.access_max_radius_m 1200, derived); under useIntermodalAccessEgress there is no nearest-stop fallback past itpt: the no-route share rose to 66.3 % on F36Daniels & Mulley (JTLU 6(2), 2013) measured 1,906 home-to-stop walks in the Sydney HTS: the mean walk to public transport is 573 m (median 518 m, upper quartile 824 m); to a train station 805 m (median 749, upper quartile 1,018 m, n = 667); to a bus stop 461 m (median 364, upper quartile 655, n = 1,084); school-bus walks 360 m. Mode of the public-transport trip is the dominant determinant - supply and stop spacing, not the walker - and the distributions are right-skewed with a tail past 1.5 km. Ewing & Cervero's meta-analysis gives a transit-demand elasticity of -0.29 to distance-to-stop (a 10 % longer walk costs about 3 % of ridership). Planning rules of thumb (400 m bus, 800 m rail; NSW's 90 %-of-households-within-400 m daytime standard) are straight-line and shorter than the observed walks.https://www.jtlu.org/index.php/jtlu/article/view/308/3382026-09-16
I16ITravel-time and speed validation: the acceptance bar for link speeds and route travel timesPARTIALcounts only (src/analyse/map_count_stations.py:47); no route-time or speed observation in fit.py (grep: none)car time 25.2 vs 17.2 minThe FHWA Traffic Analysis Toolbox Volume III (2004; Wisconsin DOT targets, Table 4) is the profession's acceptance table for a calibrated traffic model: hourly link flows within 15 % for 700-2,700 veh/h (within 100 veh/h below 700, within 400 above 2,700) in more than 85 % of cases; the sum of link flows within 5 %; GEH < 5 on individual links in more than 85 % of cases and GEH < 4 on the sum; ROUTE TRAVEL TIMES within 15 % (or one minute if higher) in more than 85 % of cases; link speeds and bottleneck queuing judged visually. The 2019 revision (TxDOT's summary) replaces the fixed bands with a two-sigma band (95 % of simulated points inside) plus two accuracy criteria applied to every metric used for calibration, and requires at least two metrics. Travel time is therefore a first-class validation target alongside counts, and a model that matches counts but not times is not accepted.https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/trafficanalysistools/tat_vol3/sect5.htm2026-09-16
J8JMobile-phone records and location-based-service data as a demand observation (OD matrices, activity diaries)OUTnone (grep)noneMobile-phone records now substitute for or complement the household survey as the demand observation at scale: Bassolas, Ramasco, Herranz & Cantu-Ros (TR-A 121, 2019) reconstructed activity diaries for the Barcelona metropolitan area from call-detail records, scaled them to census age and gender at census-tract level, ran MATSim at 10 % and VALIDATED on held-out traffic counts (9 of 11 entrances GEH < 10, the two misses attributed to excluded freight and through traffic). Nommon's practice note describes the pipeline: a continuous, region-wide sample against a household survey's ~2 % taken once a decade; expansion by classical synthetic-population techniques with census; home, work and study inferred readily, other purposes and the mode only by fusion with smartcard and classified counts, and refined in calibration. Matet, Come, Furno, Horl, Oukhellou & El Faouzi (Transportation 2024) show OD matrices from phone data improving synthetic travel demand generation (the ANR MOBITIC/PROMENADE work with eqasim). The limits are stable across sources: short trips and walking are under-detected, purpose beyond the anchors is inferred, and a privacy-aggregated zonal product needs the OD-estimation methods developed for counts.https://www.nommon.es/blog/transport-models-and-mobile-phone-data/2026-09-16
E29EWalk: the trip-length distribution and its long tail (how far people actually walk)PARTIALC.constraint.trip_length_km.walk 0.7 is reported (_fit.json trip_geometry_constraint), and seeds B.activity.short_trip_mean_km; the executed walk has no distance term and no reach bound (B.mode.walk_feasible_km 0.0 off)walk 4.54 vs 0.70 km, mean 63 minWalking trips are short and their distribution decays steeply. From the 2009 US National Household Travel Survey, Yang & Diez-Roux (AJPM 2012) report a mean walking trip of 0.7 miles and a median of 0.5 miles (about 1.1 and 0.8 km), a mean duration of 14.9 min and a median of 10 min; about 65 % of walking trips exceed 0.25 mile and only about 18 % exceed 1 mile. Distance and duration vary substantially by purpose (recreational walks are much longer) and by subgroup (lower-income people walk farther for work), and the distribution is summarised by distance-decay functions rather than a cut-off. A simulator whose walk utility is linear in time with no distance term, and whose other alternatives can fail, places mass in a multi-kilometre tail the surveys do not contain.https://digitalcommons.memphis.edu/facpubs/17034/2026-09-25

F36: 2,700,000 requests, 1,789,120 (66.3 %) no route, 200,246 of 910,875 compared chose walk: 73.7 % answered as a walk. At it.200 the selected plans hold 24,599 pt-routed walk-only trips (45.6 % of walk-only trips, mean 9.42 km, 47.5 % of walk km)walk 4.54 km / 63 min, pt -length, bike and taxi via the car-lessMATSim's routing-mode design (matsim.org news, 2019) gives every leg a routingMode attribute and binds an AnalysisMainModeIdentifier that defaults to routingMode but can be overridden for mode-share analysis; SwissRailRaptor adds a direct walk as a fallback when no pt route is found and it seems plausible. A trip the agent planned as pt but the router answered with walk legs only is therefore a pt choice executed as a walk: counted by leg modes it inflates the walk share and walk's trip length, counted by routingMode it is a pt trip that never boarded. No published benchmark states an acceptable no-route share; the design intent is that the fallback is rare.https://matsim.org/news/2019/routing-mode-helper-walk-modes/2026-09-25

Rules stated as advice that nothing enforces (14 examined)

  • The city README cap of 160 lines (HANDOVER_CONTRACT.md:31): Mumbai at 232 passes check_doc_shape under CITYSIM_CITY=mumbai.
  • Document currency for any non-default city: CI and session_gate run check_doc_currency.py for newcastle only; Mumbai is red now (1 drifted claim).
  • Reports pruned to the newest three (docs/reports/README.md:14): no check; five in the tree.
  • 25 %-only arms and the stated-cost approval (#209): the launcher refuses concurrency, heap and missing stops but not a 10 % arm or a ceiling with no recorded approval.
  • Never commit to main / branch naming never claude/*: a SessionStart reminder only; no pre-commit or pre-push hook and no branch rule in the repository.
  • A commit made outside a Claude session bypasses the hooks (#210): core.hooksPath is set only at SessionStart.
  • No co-author trailer: .githooks/commit-msg does not strip Co-Authored-By.
  • Run session_gate.py before every commit (.claude/CLAUDE.md Checks): no pre-commit hook; only the PR hook runs four document checks.
  • A position page's "What is measured" must track the open family's newest reading: the stamp is checked, the content is not (10 of 13 pages F35).
  • The brief's section 0 facts must be re-derivable: session_gate --handoff checks the commands exist, not that the stated fact still matches (brief :10 stale).
  • A secret never enters a tracked file: nothing scans .claude/settings.json (the env block holds a tracing API key, uncommitted).
  • An awaiting-run measurement is taken once its run has run (HANDOVER_CONTRACT.md:148): issue_gate resolves run names and overlays, not "F36's arm 0" family phrasing, and never considers a stopped arm.
  • Sandbox domains carry a provenance record ("A new source means adding its domain there and a provenance record"): nothing checks that each allowed domain has one; Nagpur hosts remain after the rollback.
  • Record sections follow the handoff template (title with date, session ordinal and issues): 9.178-9.200 do not; check_doc_shape checks order, cap and index only.

In-flight work seen in the tree

.claude/settings.json carries an uncommitted env block with a tracing API key (value not reproduced here). With tracing on, session transcripts leave the machine. It is not committed and must not be; recommendation 11.

Since the last report, and the report process itself

Of the previous report's 10 findings, 3 are fixed (the sampling capacity regex, goal_met coverage, the four-name fleet capacity) and 7 remain, the taxi wait among them (now ranked 3). Of its 8 recommendations 2 were taken; its recommendation to resolve the package audit before a new arm was not, and F36 arm 0 launched with check_package.py failing. New this pass: the missing external tier, the misderived access ceiling (measured across every run on disk), the pricer's dead-host setup, the host-restart exposure. The reference library gained 3 projects (Greater Jakarta, Okanagan, CALM New York) and 2 factor rows (E29 walk distance, F7 the pt no-route walk); no project in the field validates every mode's ridership. The factor ledger at HEAD: IN 41, PARTIAL 48, INERT 1, ASC 2, OUT 11.

verdict

FOLLOWED, AT THE INSTRUMENT LEVEL; NOT AT THE GOAL LEVEL. Of 225 recommendations over 13 reports, 174 are taken (77 %, a handful only in part), 4 overtaken, 16 repeated and 31 open. The first ten reports' rows are 144 of 177 taken; the ledger era (#11-#13) is 30 of 48 - and report #13's 8 were 2 taken, 5 open, 1 overtaken, with its rec 7 ('resolve the package audit before a new arm') plainly not followed: F36 arm 0 launched on 23 Sep over 114 check_package failures. What gets taken, fast (usually the same or next PR), is what a session can do alone: readers, launchers, gates, checks, documents, hidden constants - and several of those were real correctness wins (the holdout leak into the count targets, #152; the count map on the wrong roads, #176; the reader that read heavy rail 0, #201; unscaled standing room, #240). What never gets taken is what needs an external party, an approval or a machine: the replication band (issued 8 times, still 0.0), the TfNSW request (7 times, 'Not yet sent'), a second reviewer (3 times, 0 reviews on 90 PRs), build timing (3 times). DID FOLLOWING THEM MOVE THE GOAL COUNT? Not demonstrably. The count went 0 -> 2 once, between the F32 result (9 Sep: car +11.3 %, motorbike +12.5 %) and the F35 result (14 Sep: +9.6 %, -5.6 %), across a family boundary that bundled the passenger-on-ride demand (#177), the footpath network (#194 - report #9's rec 20) and the engines' routing (#195, not a recommendation); the step cannot be attributed, and car sits 0.4 pp inside the band. Since then it has not moved: the two recommended model controls that were run (routers pair, #8-#11's top ask; scoring pair, #12's rec 1) cost 53.16 machine hours and read as nulls; the roots rebuild the reports asked for from #9 onwards landed on 22 Sep (#254) and its only arm was killed at iteration 237 of 250. CADENCE: 13 reports in 16 days is too many - four on 7 Sep, two on 14 Sep - and the repeats are now the core of every recommendation set; the once-per-reading rule (11 Sep) is being kept (gaps 2.2, 0.6, 1.6, 2.5, 7.0 days). AGAINST THIS REPORT: any recommendation below that re-asks the replication band (9th), the TfNSW request (8th), a second reviewer (4th), build timing (4th), the package audit before an arm (2nd) or travel-time validation (2nd) is a repeat, and should either be converted into a decision the user takes once (lane.json) or be dropped.

finding
None of the last 15 PRs moved the goal count; it has been 2 of 12 on every result since 14 Sep. Two PRs ran a model control and both were nulls (53.16 machine hours); four changed the Newcastle model (standing room, transit PCE, the Java fold, the roots rebuild) and only the roots rebuild reached an arm - killed at 237 of 250, so its visibly different levels (ride -13.7 %, walk -18.6 %) are not a result and cannot be differenced against F35. Five were Mumbai-only on a host that cannot read Mumbai (D15), and four were instruments, documents or harness. Work aimed at the goal's metric in the last 11 days: one rebuild, one killed arm.
whole_history
Across all 90 PRs the goal count at a result moved once (0 -> 2, the F32 -> F35 boundary: #177 + #194 + #195); at gates, bus came inside at F22 (#105 fares), car at F28 (#146) and F31 (#160). Every other move was inside a family's noise or at a reading that was not a result.

Recommendations, ranked

Ranked by what each would prevent or move × how cheap it is. A repeat tag marks one an earlier report already issued; the process audit counts them against this report too.

  1. Write the external boundary tier again, and pin plans persons to the chains report by tier. model opens a family
    6,103 boundary agents (12,206 weekday trips) are absent from F36, the only family built after the refactor; a check would have caught it the day it happened.
    change: src/build/build_matsim_plans.py:1246 - B1 lookup for the core tier only; tests/check_package.py asserts persons per tier equal _activity_chains_report.json; a unit test of write_person per tier. · guard: the new tier assertion; the per-tier unit test
  2. Derive the pt access ceiling as the beeline finder's real reach, not 1,000 + 200 m. model opens a family
    It doubles the no-route share (38.8-39.4 % -> 66.3 %) and hands pt choosers 9 km walks; walk runs 6.5x its observed length and pt trips come out too short.
    change: RUN.transit_router.access_max_radius_m: identity = max over activity locations of the distance to the nearest stop + the extension radius, computed by the assembler from the run's own stops and facilities; record it and supersede the old identity. · guard: diagnose_pt_routing.py bracket equals the run's own ptDirectWalk counter within 2 pp
  3. Make the taxi wait real: delay the served departure by the fleet's wait and let the score see it. model repeat ×1 opens a family
    A 16-minute mean wait nobody experiences keeps taxi at +107 %.
    change: src/java/citysim/TaxiFleetEngine.java:243 - apply wait to the leg's departure (restored after the mobsim, as the refusal remode is); retire the constant's folded 5-minute wait (C.taxi.wait_min) in the same change. · guard: a probe test on the engine; the log's meanWait against the executed wait
  4. Explain the remaining ~39 % of pt trips that find no connection even without the cap. model
    78 % of them persist at 15:00, the busiest hour; either the 300 m transfer walk splits the network or trip ends lie where no service runs - the two call for different fixes.
    change: extend src/analyse/diagnose_pt_routing.py with the no-route split by trip-end distance band and by transfer-walk radius (300/500/800 m), read-only on F36 arm 0. · guard: the diagnostic's JSON carries the split
  5. Guard the host: refuse a launch while a restart is pending or updates are not paused past the cost ceiling; close a host death as a crash; allow a warm start after the cutoff. code
    A forced update restart killed a 42 h arm 13 iterations short; it has happened twice in ten days.
    change: src/run/run_matsim.py (a refuse_unsafe_host beside refuse_concurrent_arm), procs.boot_time for the crash rule, warm_start_overrides for post-cutoff checkpoints. · guard: unit tests on the refusal and on a post-cutoff warm start
  6. Price an arm from its own clock, never from wall minus iterations. code
    The next quote reads 62.9 h against ~25.6 h.
    change: src/analyse/arm_cost.py:193 - setup from the stopwatch's it.0 BEGIN minus launch; the same cap for _run.json wall_s and the machine-hours aggregate. · guard: a unit test with a dead-host run
  7. Close the four silent paths on the result path. code
    A raw override that matches nothing is recorded as applied; a re-extraction reads today's registry; an all-infeasible search crashes without a record; min/max arguments hide constants from the ledger.
    change: run_matsim.py:148 setp refuses 0 or >1 matches; extract_metrics.py:353 reads the run's _config.json; calibrate.py:630 initialises best_tag; check_hardcoding.py:1208 drops the min/max exemption and the age ceiling 95 is declared. · guard: one unit test each; check_hardcoding.py --strict at 0
  8. Let every reader read a stopped arm. code
    measure_bound_trips.py and mode_by_demographics.py require output_persons, which only a completed run has, so #86 #107 #145 cannot be measured on F36 arm 0.
    change: one persons helper in iteration_reading.py (the run's own plans.xml.gz attributes when output_persons is absent), used by both readers. · guard: a unit test on a stopped-arm fixture
  9. Split the god functions and retire the mechanical staging. code opens a family
    Maintainability is 2-3 in every area: CitysimControler.assemble 607 lines, RidePairingEngine.notifyBeforeMobsim 566, and 34 staged Python functions that pass 2-29 names through a namespace under a false docstring - the refactor that dropped the external tier.
    change: typed contexts in build_matsim_plans.py; retire extract_loop_body.py and split_stages.py; split the two Java methods (Java changes open a family - do it with the next family). · guard: byte-identical plans on the committed demand, EXECUTED, per tier
  10. Test what decides a reading. code
    Testability is 2-3: write_person per tier, build_population, iteration_trips, measure_iteration_modes and the taxi and ride engines have no unit test.
    change: tests/unit/ - one file per module, a small fixture per tier; a Java probe per engine. · guard: the tests themselves; code_metrics' uncovered list shrinks
  11. Refuse a secret in a tracked file. process
    A tracing API key sits uncommitted in the tracked .claude/settings.json; no check would stop a handoff from publishing it.
    change: a pattern check in the commit-msg/pre-commit hook and session_gate.py; move the key to the gitignored .claude/settings.local.json. · guard: the hook refuses a staged key
  12. Close the issues the record has overtaken, and let the issue gate see a stopped arm. process
    9 open issues are overtaken (#214 fixed on 16 September); the gate reports 0 measurements due because issues name a family, not a run.
    change: src/run/issue_gate.py resolves family names through docs/run_families.json and accepts a stopped arm's record; close or relabel on evidence. · guard: issue_gate lists measurement-due rows
  13. Read walk's trip length after the access fix before adding any walk distance cost. model
    The literature (Yang & Diez-Roux 2012: mean 0.7 mi) and the bike rule of §9.211 both point at a walk distance term, but most walk km today are routing fallbacks; a cost laid on them would be a compensating constant.
    change: after recommendation 2, read walk km split by routingMode; only then derive C.scoring.marginal_utility_of_distance_per_m.walk from the HTS mean if self-chosen walks still run long. · guard: walk km by routingMode in _metrics.json
  14. Do not resume F36 arm 0; open F37 on recommendations 1-3 and price it on this build. process
    Three defects sit under F36 (the missing tier, the access cap, the unexperienced taxi wait); completing its last 13 iterations would buy a result on a demand already known to be wrong.
    change: F37 opens on the fixes; its 4-iteration probe prices the arm (arm_cost.py after recommendation 6). · guard: the family ledger records the boundary
  15. Send the TfNSW bespoke-table request. data repeat ×7
    The four cells (mode x age, trip length by mode, occupancy by purpose, the unfolded Other) exist on no public channel; trip length by mode is what walk and bike now need.
    change: the drafted request (#50); the user sends it. · guard: docs/lane.json D2
  16. Measure the replication band. model repeat ×8
    CAL.objective.replication_band_pp ships 0.0; without it no deviation can be told from noise.
    change: three short seeded arms on the next family. · guard: the objective refuses a 0.0 band

Appendix

Reproduce: the three collectors under .claude/skills/project-report/scripts/, the six lanes' JSON, then render_report.py. The no-route series: every results/raw/*/matsim.log tail, last ptDirectWalk line. The offline re-route: python src/analyse/diagnose_pt_routing.py --run 20260923T034632_250it_25pct --sample 3000. Search rounds: field 7 rounds, 23 calls; factors 8 calls. Depth of read is partial in every code area and declared there.
